description: Team Estrella is a team of high school students from Bangladesh, with our Team Leader, Sabiha Akter Nib. Participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, our team brings together three Grade 7 students with complementary strengths in data, software development, design, and research.
summary:
ASTERRO is a planetary analogue intelligence platform that identifies Earth locations with measurable environmental similarities to the Moon and Mars. It helps researchers, planetary scientists, mission planners, educators, and future explorers understand unfamiliar planetary environments by learning from conditions on Earth. Preparing for exploration beyond Earth requires understanding environmental conditions, terrain, temperature behaviour, and differences between planetary surfaces. However, comparing worlds is challenging because datasets are often incomplete, collected at different scales, and measured using different instruments.

ASTERRO addresses this through a deterministic, explainable scoring engine that evaluates 76,781 valid Earth cells against planetary fingerprints across six dimensions: aridity, annual temperature range, elevation, slope, surface roughness, and thermal behaviour. It identifies potential analogue locations, calculates environmental similarity, and reveals the evidence behind each result. Beyond analogue discovery, ASTERRO offers interactive planetary exploration, environmental comparisons, spatial analysis, temporal evolution, uncertainty assessment, mission-planning profiles, scientific reproducibility, and educational tools. By revealing both similarities and differences, ASTERRO transforms planetary data into accessible, explainable, and reproducible scientific insights.
details:
WHAT DOES IT EXACTLY DO?

ASTERRO is designed to identify and investigate Earth's environmental analogues for locations on the Moon and Mars. Instead of comparing planetary landscapes through photographs alone, it compares measurable environmental characteristics and reveals how closely different places resemble one another.

The platform begins with a planetary destination. Users can select a Moon or Mars target, including Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, and other catalogued planetary locations. They can also explore different mission and research objectives through configurable analytical profiles.

Once a destination is selected, ASTERRO evaluates Earth's valid environmental cells using its deterministic scoring engine, currently identified as tai-sim-1.0.0. The engine compares the selected planetary fingerprint with Earth's environmental data across six dimensions:

  • Aridity
  • Annual temperature range
  • Elevation
  • Slope
  • Surface roughness
  • Thermal behaviour

Each dimension contributes to the overall environmental similarity calculation according to its assigned weight. Users can adjust six individual weight controls to explore how different environmental priorities affect the results. A minimum weighted data-coverage requirement of 80% ensures that insufficient data do not silently produce misleading scores.

ASTERRO evaluates 76,781 valid Earth cells and identifies potential analogue locations through a deterministic ranking process. To encourage geographically distinct results, its baseline ranking applies a 300-kilometre separation rule between selected candidates.

The result is not simply a list of locations. Every candidate can be investigated through its planetary fingerprint, similarity percentage, individual dimension scores, strongest matches, mismatches, data coverage, and evidence quality.

THE HOME PAGE AND PLANETARY DISCOVERY

The home page introduces users to ASTERRO and provides access to its main analytical and exploration capabilities.

Users can begin by searching Earth, selecting a planetary destination, exploring a guided discovery, or viewing the current analogue rankings. A guided discovery helps new users understand real results from the dataset through step-by-step explanations.

The destination selector allows users to choose the Moon, Mars, or available planetary targets. The platform also provides separate Explore Mode and Research Mode experiences, allowing users to move between accessible discovery and deeper scientific investigation.

Users can explore the results through an interactive globe and map interface, switch between geographical views, inspect individual Earth cells, and navigate to potential analogue locations.

ASTERRO also supports five interface languages: English, Bengali, Spanish, French, and German.



SEARCH EARTH AND ANALOGUE RANKING

The Search Earth feature allows users to investigate the planet and discover potential environmental analogues for a selected planetary target.

After selecting a destination and analytical profile, users can examine the ranked Earth locations and explore how their environmental characteristics compare with the target.

The ranking interface presents candidate locations, their similarity percentages, geographical information, and relevant analytical details. The 300-kilometre separation rule helps prevent the baseline list from being dominated by neighbouring cells.



Users can select a candidate to inspect its environmental fingerprint, compare individual dimensions, identify mismatches, and investigate the data behind its score.

The system also supports different mission-oriented weighting profiles, allowing users to examine how the ranking changes when the research objective changes.

PLANETARY FINGERPRINT

Every planetary target and selected Earth candidate can be examined through its environmental fingerprint.

A planetary fingerprint represents measurable environmental characteristics in a structured format. ASTERRO displays the six baseline dimensions and allows users to examine the target and Earth measurements side by side.

The fingerprint interface includes:

  • Planetary and Earth environmental values.
  • Normalised fingerprint visualisations.
  • Individual dimension similarity.
  • Overall analogue similarity percentage.
  • Match and mismatch indicators.
  • Analogue DNA, showing the environmental characteristics that define a candidate.
  • Data-quality indicators.
  • Missing-data information.
  • Dimension-level explanations.

The Difference Lens helps users understand where two environments are similar, partly similar, different, or unknown. Rather than presenting only an overall percentage, it explains which environmental characteristics support the comparison and which do not.

This is particularly important because two locations may have a similar overall score while having very different environmental characteristics.


SIX ENVIRONMENTAL DIMENSIONS AND WEIGHT CUSTOMISATION

ASTERRO allows users to adjust the importance of its six environmental dimensions.

For example, a researcher interested in terrain may assign greater importance to slope and surface roughness, while another researcher may prioritise aridity and thermal behaviour.

The platform recalculates the analytical ranking according to the selected weights. This allows users to investigate different environmental priorities without changing the underlying source measurements.

The standard baseline scoring method remains deterministic and reproducible. Missing data do not increase a candidate's score, and the minimum 80% weighted coverage requirement prevents insufficiently supported comparisons from being treated as complete.

ANALOGUE ANALYSIS AND SCIENTIFIC EVIDENCE

ASTERRO provides several ways to understand, investigate, and verify its analytical results.

Trace Results exposes the evidence behind an individual result, including its environmental measurements, dimension-level contributions, and relevant scoring information.

Reproduce Results provides the configuration and information required to reproduce an analytical result. This includes the planetary target, environmental weights, profile, algorithm version, normalisation, and applicable rules.

The Analogue Analysis Report brings the result together into a structured scientific report.

Users can also explore:

  • Similarity analysis.
  • Environmental coverage.
  • Individual dimension contributions.
  • Scientific interpretation.
  • Match and mismatch analysis.
  • Data quality and uncertainty.
  • Evidence and source information.
  • Result reproducibility.

The purpose is to make the analytical process understandable rather than asking users to accept a similarity percentage without evidence.



ANALOGUE CONSTELLATIONS

The Analogue Constellations feature explores relationships between different Earth environments.

It examines the top 800 candidate cells and uses k-means clustering to group locations with related environmental characteristics. The current configuration uses three clusters, selected using a silhouette score of 0.378.

The resulting groups are described through their environmental characteristics, including temperature, aridity, elevation, and terrain.

Users can explore the different environmental groups, their geographical distributions, the number of cells in each group, and their average analogue scores.

ASTERRO also provides a planetary analogue graph that connects planetary targets with their leading Earth candidates. The graph represents relationships through computed similarity, allowing users to explore connections between different destinations and Earth environments.

The latitude distribution analysis shows where candidate locations occur in relation to Earth's valid land area. It helps identify geographical patterns and latitude bands where candidates are overrepresented or absent.



ANALOGUE EVOLUTION AND CHANGE

Environmental conditions are not always constant. ASTERRO therefore includes an Analogue Evolution feature that investigates how the similarity of a selected Earth location changes over time.

The feature presents yearly similarity results and identifies whether a candidate remains relatively stable under the available temporal data.

For example, the Planalto do Mato Grosso region in Brazil can be examined through its analogue evolution. In the current implementation, the thermal criterion varies annually using MODIS observations from 2016 to 2025, while climate and terrain use their fixed climatologies.

The stability classification is based on the range of yearly similarity scores. A candidate is classified as stable when that range is no greater than two percentage points.

This allows users to investigate whether an environmental analogue remains consistent or changes over the observed period.

TEMPERATURE EXTREMES

ASTERRO includes an extended temperature analysis that investigates environmental conditions beyond the six standard baseline dimensions.

The Temperature Extremes feature uses a separate, versioned fingerprint configuration called explore-ext-thermal-v1. It applies the baseline scoring formula to nine conditions: the six standard dimensions, daytime surface temperature, nighttime surface temperature, and mean air temperature.

Users can investigate temperature-related environmental patterns across different planetary targets and Earth locations.

This extended analysis operates separately from the standard baseline. It does not silently change the original six-dimensional scoring method or its existing rankings.

PLANETARY PROCESS EXPLORER

ASTERRO explores planetary processes as well as geographical locations.

The Planetary Process Explorer allows users to investigate environmental processes that can be studied on Earth and examine their relevance to lunar and Martian environments.

Depending on available data, processes are classified according to whether they can be searched directly, examined through indirect indicators, or described as research topics requiring additional datasets.

Searchable processes include:

  • Thermal cycling and thermal weathering.
  • Freeze-thaw conditions at the surface.
  • Hyper-arid surface environments.
  • Steep and rugged terrain.
  • Cold, dry, high-altitude deserts.
  • Extreme cold.

Processes explored through indirect indicators include:

  • Permafrost processes.
  • Glacial and ice processes.
  • Dust storms.
  • Aeolian erosion and dust transport.
  • Salt deposition.
  • Sedimentation.
  • Fluvial landforms.
  • Surface erosion and material transport.

Other processes, including volcanism and lava tubes, impact cratering, and water-driven alteration, are presented as descriptive research topics because the required integrated measurements are not available for direct global searching.

This distinction helps users understand both what the current data can investigate and where additional observations are needed.



BEYOND THE FAMILIAR

The Beyond the Familiar feature explores Earth's less frequently considered environmental analogue candidates.

It presents the leading 100 distinct locations for the selected planetary target and current weights, excluding locations within 300 kilometres of frequently cited analogue sites.

The feature helps researchers investigate environments beyond commonly referenced analogue locations and identify candidates that may deserve further study.

Users can explore geographical locations, environmental scores, and the strongest and weakest dimensions of each candidate.

The feature does not claim that a location is scientifically undiscovered or that it has never been studied. Establishing that would require a dedicated literature review. Instead, it provides a systematic way to explore locations outside the selected reference-site list.

NOVELTY AND DIVERSITY

The Novelty and Diversity feature allows users to examine how analogue rankings change under different geographical and environmental diversity rules.

Users can compare the standard 300-kilometre baseline with alternative approaches, including:

  • Custom geographical separation distances.
  • Environmental variety.
  • One candidate per country.

The feature also investigates how each candidate relates to frequently cited analogue locations.

It distinguishes between candidates near known reference sites, locations farther away but environmentally similar to listed sites, and locations that are both environmentally unusual and geographically distinct from those references.

Rarity is assessed through environmental similarity relationships with other Earth cells. Missing data are not treated as evidence of novelty.

The feature helps users explore different ways of selecting diverse analogue candidates without modifying the original baseline ranking.

ENVIRONMENTAL PATTERNS AND UNUSUAL COMBINATIONS

ASTERRO uses unsupervised environmental analysis to investigate broader patterns across Earth's environments.

The Environmental Patterns feature groups Earth cells using twelve coarse environmental variables and compares the resulting groups with the Köppen-Geiger climate classification as an interpretable reference.

The current analysis identifies eight environmental groups, each described through characteristics such as temperature, aridity, and surface roughness.

The system also identifies unusual environmental combinations using an isolation-forest anomaly score.

These combinations may contain individually ordinary environmental values that become unusual when considered together.

ASTERRO provides stability and sensitivity analysis for these patterns, including comparisons across different random initialisations, input changes, and geographical distributions.

Because these are statistical patterns in coarse environmental data, they are not presented as confirmed geological discoveries or proof of specific landforms.

SURPRISE ME

Surprise Me provides an interactive way to discover unexpected connections between Earth and planetary environments.

It draws discoveries from real analytical results and encourages users to investigate the evidence behind them.

Discovery categories include:

  • Unexpected Mars analogues.
  • Unexpected Moon analogues.
  • Unusual thermal environments.
  • Unexpected polar environments.
  • Hidden environmental combinations.
  • Underrepresented geographical regions.
  • Locations strongly matching one condition.
  • Unusual geological connections.
  • Water-history connections.
  • Dust and wind processes.
  • Subsurface discovery topics.

The feature also includes discovery challenges that encourage users to investigate specific environmental relationships.

Examples include finding Martian-like terrain with very different thermal behaviour, exploring dry and rugged environments, identifying strongly seasonal rainfall, comparing polar-night conditions, and discovering locations that match one environmental condition while differing in others.

Users can maintain a Discovery Journal to track their investigations, including mismatches identified, scores interpreted, uncertainty examined, results reproduced, and research questions explored.

The discovery points and badges reward careful investigation rather than high similarity scores. They do not affect analytical results and are stored locally in the browser.



LEARN: PLANETARY ANALOGUES IN SEVEN STEPS

ASTERRO includes an educational learning experience that introduces users to the scientific principles behind planetary analogues.

The learning section explains the meaning of planetary analogues and why researchers use Earth environments to study other worlds.

It guides users through seven essential questions:

  1. What is a planetary analogue?
  2. Why do scientists use Earth analogues?
  3. How are lunar and Martian environments measured?
  4. What makes a useful landing-site analogue?
  5. How does environmental similarity work?
  6. Why can two places that look alike be different?
  7. What are the limitations of Earth analogues?

The educational experience helps users understand that an analogue is always partial. A location may resemble Mars in dryness or terrain while differing in atmospheric pressure, radiation, gravity, or other planetary conditions.



PLANETARY ATLAS

The Planetary Atlas provides a catalogue of 33 planetary targets: 18 on Mars and 15 on the Moon.

Users can explore targets by planet, search by name, geographical feature, or mission, filter by target type, and apply minimum data-readiness levels.

Each target includes its geographical location, available environmental fingerprint, measurement status, and readiness classification.

The atlas distinguishes between directly measured values, proxy values, missing information, and unavailable measurements. It does not estimate missing values simply to create a complete fingerprint.

The four readiness levels are:

  • L1 — Catalogued: verified basic metadata and an authoritative reference.
  • L2 — Partially Characterized: documented data are associated with a complete measurement window, but a complete compatible comparison is not yet supported.
  • L3 — Analytically Comparable: applicable criteria have accepted direct or proxy evidence, with at least three direct criteria.
  • L4 — Reproducible: a versioned fingerprint, documented scripts, and successful offline regeneration of every direct value.

Users can inspect individual targets, compare multiple targets, and examine their environmental characteristics.

The catalogue includes locations such as Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Elysium Planitia, Utopia Planitia, Gusev Crater, Hellas Planitia, Valles Marineris, Olympus Mons, Arcadia Planitia, and other Martian regions, alongside lunar locations such as Shackleton Crater and other lunar research targets.

The atlas also provides geographical context through planetary shaded-relief visualisations. Contextual relief is not treated as a measurement for the baseline comparison.



PLANETARY COMPARISON LAB

The Planetary Comparison Lab allows users to compare multiple Moon and Mars targets criterion by criterion.

Users can select two or more analytical targets and examine their environmental fingerprints side by side.

The comparison interface includes:

  • Fingerprints side by side.
  • Dimension-level comparison.
  • Compatibility matrix.
  • Mismatch Explorer.
  • Mismatch maps.
  • Mismatch signatures.
  • Constellation analysis.
  • Multi-target aggregate analysis.

The compatibility matrix identifies whether a comparison is based on direct measurements, proxy measurements, or unavailable information.

Aggregated comparisons use only criteria that are directly available for every selected target. Criteria that cannot be compared consistently are explicitly excluded.

The lab also provides different multi-target analytical approaches, including minimum-score comparisons, mean-score summaries, and Pareto analysis.

This helps users understand whether an Earth environment resembles several planetary targets simultaneously or performs differently across individual targets.


RESEARCH LABORATORY

ASTERRO includes a dedicated Research Laboratory for deeper scientific investigation.

The Research Lab guides users through an eight-step analytical workflow:

  1. Choose a Moon or Mars target.
  2. Choose an Earth candidate.
  3. Compare environmental dimensions.
  4. Adjust analytical weights.
  5. Explore differences and missing data.
  6. Examine scientific evidence.
  7. Interpret and apply the findings.
  8. Reproduce the result.

The workflow connects the selected planetary target, Earth candidate, environmental measurements, analytical configuration, evidence, interpretation, and reproducibility.

Beyond the guided workflow, the Research Lab provides fourteen deeper research modules that operate alongside the baseline scoring engine rather than silently changing its original results.

These modules include:

1. Analogue Robustness Laboratory

Tests whether a candidate's ranking remains stable when analytical weights change. It supports one-at-a-time weight variations, full-factorial experiments, seeded random sampling, and criterion-ablation experiments.

2. Multi-Objective Analogue Discovery

Investigates candidates across multiple environmental objectives and identifies Pareto-optimal results without forcing every dimension into one single winning score.

3. Spatial Analogue Microclimate Atlas

Explores spatial variation around selected locations, including neighbourhood information, target windows, and available terrain sub-cell characteristics.

4. Planetary Uncertainty Explorer

Investigates uncertainty in environmental measurements and comparisons, quantifying uncertainty where data allow and describing limitations where numerical quantification is unavailable.

5. Analogue Failure-Mode Laboratory

Examines where an analogue comparison may fail, including weak dimensions, missing evidence, incompatible measurements, and limitations in the available data.

6. Planetary Evidence Graph

Connects planetary targets, Earth candidates, analytical results, and evidence records through a structured evidence graph.

7. Cross-Planet Evidence Comparator

Compares environmental evidence across different planetary targets and examines how compatible measurements support or limit cross-planet comparisons.

8. Planetary Analogue Evolution Observatory

Investigates how analogue similarity changes over time using available temporal observations and documented analytical configurations.

9. Mission Requirement Translator

Translates user-defined mission requirements into environmental criteria that can be examined using ASTERRO's available measurements.

10. Observation Value Engine

Provides qualitative evidence-priority guidance to help identify which additional observations could be most useful for reducing uncertainty. It does not claim to calculate a fully formal value-of-information result.

11. Analogue Research Mission Planner

Connects the outputs of ASTERRO's analytical modules to support structured research planning and investigation.

12. Scientific Reproducibility Vault

Stores research configurations and reproducibility records in browser storage, with available offline replay capabilities for supported analytical experiments.

13. Scientific Review

Provides deterministic scientific review using evidence records, methods, assumptions, provenance, and limitations.

14. Research Copilot

Provides an AI-assisted research interface through the Anthropic API to help users investigate planetary analogue concepts and understand available scientific evidence. AI-generated explanations are an assistance layer and do not replace the deterministic scoring engine or scientific evidence.

The Research Laboratory is designed to make ASTERRO useful not only for discovering candidate locations but also for testing, challenging, comparing, and reproducing scientific interpretations.



MISSION PLANNING

The Mission Planning section explores how leading Earth analogue candidates perform under different planetary exploration and operational objectives.

Instead of assuming that one location is the best analogue for every purpose, ASTERRO allows users to investigate candidates through different mission and operations profiles.

Available profiles include:

  • General analogue.
  • Rover mobility.
  • EVA training.
  • Thermal testing.
  • Habitat operations.
  • Science instrument testing.

Each profile uses its own environmental weighting configuration. Consequently, a location that ranks highly for rover mobility may not rank equally highly for thermal testing or habitat operations.

The Mission Planning section also includes:

Mission and Operations Profiles: Compare candidate locations under different exploration objectives.

Portfolio: Select a group of locations and investigate how they collectively cover different environmental requirements.

Trajectory: Explore how the analogue field and candidate rankings change through time.

Scenarios: Examine alternative weighting configurations and understand how different priorities affect candidate selection.

Mission Requirement Translator: Translate user-defined environmental thresholds into measurable analytical requirements.

The system also identifies mission profiles that cannot yet be built reliably because essential measurements are unavailable. It does not replace missing geological, dust, mineralogical, subsurface, or human-environment data with unrelated measurements.

Mission profiles represent environmental similarity for a research objective. They do not certify landing-site safety, mission readiness, or operational suitability.



LOCAL IMPACT

The Local Impact feature connects planetary analogue research with locations on Earth.

Users can select a geographical location and investigate its environmental characteristics in relation to a chosen Moon or Mars target.

The feature provides:

  • Local environmental fingerprints.
  • Nearby Earth cells.
  • Environmental measurements around the selected location.
  • Nearby named geographical features.
  • Local analogue discoveries.
  • Exploration relevance.
  • Science domains.
  • Research objectives.
  • Environmental layers.
  • Available mineral-occurrence information.
  • Local analytical reports.
  • Saved places.

Users can explore the environmental conditions surrounding a location, examine nearby candidate analogues, and investigate which research activities may be supported by the available evidence.

The Exploration Relevance section considers objectives such as landing research, rover mobility, navigation, robotic operations, instrument deployment, EVA training, habitat operations, construction technology, resource prospecting, geological fieldwork, subsurface exploration, environmental monitoring, and educational planetary science.

The feature also explains what Earth cannot reproduce exactly, including gravity, atmospheric pressure, atmospheric composition, radiation, and other planetary conditions.

Science domains are presented with their own data availability and evidence status. A domain may be available, partially supported, awaiting data, or not supported by local samples.

Users can save places and revisit their local investigations.

Local Impact does not certify a location's physical safety, accessibility, permits, geological suitability, or mission readiness. It evaluates the available environmental evidence and clearly communicates its limitations.



RESEARCH COPILOT AND ANALOGUE TRANSLATOR

ASTERRO provides additional assistance for understanding planetary research through its AI-assisted Research Copilot and Analogue Translator.

Research Copilot uses the Anthropic API to support users as they investigate planetary analogue concepts and ask questions about the available research.

Analogue Translator helps explain complex planetary environmental concepts in more accessible language, making it easier to understand scientific terminology, environmental comparisons, and the meaning of analytical results.

These tools are intended to support scientific learning and interpretation. They do not replace the deterministic scoring engine, source measurements, or reproducible analytical methods.


EVIDENCE, DATA AND TRUST

Scientific transparency is a central part of ASTERRO.

The Evidence, Data and Trust section allows users to investigate the information behind the platform's results and understand how its datasets are processed and used.

It includes:

  • Evidence.
  • Data inventory.
  • Data integration status.
  • Data gaps.
  • Source information.
  • Processing information.
  • Methodology.
  • Limitations.
  • Reproducibility information.
  • Trust Centre.

ASTERRO distinguishes between measured, derived, inferred, assumed, unavailable, and unvalidated information.

These categories are not interchangeable. A derived value is not a direct observation, an assumption is not a measurement, and an unavailable dataset cannot be treated as evidence.

The platform also distinguishes between data used in the baseline scoring engine, data used in additional analytical modules, contextual visualisation sources, and datasets that are described but not yet integrated.

This makes it possible for users to understand not only what ASTERRO can calculate, but also what it cannot currently establish.


EXPORT, OFFLINE ACCESS AND DATA INTEGRITY

ASTERRO includes export and reproducibility capabilities that support further research and independent investigation.

Users can export supported analytical configurations and results, including structured JSON output where available.

The platform also supports offline caching for accessible application resources and provides SHA-256 integrity verification for supported data assets.

These capabilities help users revisit research results, inspect configurations, and verify the integrity of available data files.

HOW DOES IT WORK?

ASTERRO operates through a deterministic environmental comparison framework.

First, the user selects a planetary target and an analytical objective. The platform retrieves the corresponding planetary environmental fingerprint and compares it with the available Earth environmental measurements.

Earth is represented through 76,781 valid environmental cells. Each cell contains measurable environmental characteristics that can be compared with the selected planetary target.

The baseline scoring engine evaluates six dimensions: aridity, annual temperature range, elevation, slope, surface roughness, and thermal behaviour.

The environmental dimensions are normalised and weighted according to the selected analytical profile. The system then calculates the similarity between the planetary target and each eligible Earth cell.

A minimum weighted data-coverage requirement of 80% is applied. Missing information is not treated as a positive match, and cells that do not satisfy the required coverage are not silently assigned misleading results.

The system ranks eligible Earth cells according to their calculated similarity. It then applies the baseline 300-kilometre geographical separation rule to identify distinct candidate locations.

Users can explore the resulting candidates through the interactive globe, map, rankings, planetary fingerprints, and research interfaces.

Every result can be investigated through its dimension-level evidence, data quality, mismatches, configuration, and reproducibility information.

Additional research modules operate alongside the baseline engine. These modules investigate uncertainty, robustness, spatial patterns, temporal evolution, multi-objective comparisons, environmental diversity, and mission-oriented applications without silently altering the standard baseline score.

The overall architecture is designed to make planetary analogue discovery explainable, reproducible, and scientifically cautious.

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

  • Discovering Potential Planetary Analogues: Identifies Earth locations with measurable environmental similarities to selected Moon and Mars targets, helping researchers explore possible analogue environments.
  • Evidence-Based Planetary Research: Connects every analytical result with environmental measurements, dimension-level comparisons, data quality, and supporting evidence.
  • Explainable Scientific Analysis: Shows why a location receives a particular similarity score instead of presenting an unexplained ranking.
  • Understanding Environmental Differences: Helps users identify where an Earth location matches a planetary target and where the comparison breaks down.
  • More Flexible Research: Allows users to adjust environmental weights and investigate different mission and scientific objectives.
  • Improved Scientific Reproducibility: Provides traceable results, reproducibility configurations, analytical reports, and supported offline verification.
  • Uncertainty and Robustness Investigation: Helps researchers understand whether rankings remain stable under changing weights and where additional evidence may be required.
  • Spatial and Temporal Environmental Understanding: Provides tools to explore environmental clusters, geographical distributions, unusual combinations, and changes through time.
  • Mission-Oriented Exploration Research: Supports the investigation of rover mobility, EVA training, thermal testing, habitat operations, and scientific instrument testing through different environmental profiles.
  • Planetary Science Education: Makes complex planetary concepts more accessible through guided discoveries, seven-step learning, interactive visualisations, and scientific explanations.
  • Local Environmental Research: Connects local Earth environments with planetary research through Local Impact, nearby candidate analysis, and science-domain information.
  • Exploration Beyond Familiar Locations: Helps researchers investigate less frequently considered analogue candidates and explore environmental diversity.
  • Scientific Transparency: Communicates missing data, measurement limitations, assumptions, proxy values, and unavailable evidence rather than presenting incomplete information as certainty.
  • Multilingual Accessibility: Supports five interface languages, making planetary research more accessible to users from different linguistic backgrounds.
  • A Foundation for Future Research: Provides a structured platform that can expand as additional planetary observations, Earth datasets, and validated analytical methods become available.

WHAT DO WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE?

  • Make planetary analogue discovery more systematic, accessible, and reproducible.
  • Help researchers identify Earth environments that share measurable characteristics with the Moon and Mars.
  • Support scientific investigation through transparent environmental comparisons.
  • Encourage the use of evidence rather than visual resemblance alone when studying planetary environments.
  • Improve understanding of environmental similarities, mismatches, uncertainty, and data limitations.
  • Provide a foundation for investigating different planetary exploration and operational objectives.
  • Encourage further research into environmental processes that occur on Earth and other planetary bodies.
  • Make planetary science more accessible to students, educators, researchers, and future explorers.
  • Expand the platform as new planetary observations and compatible Earth datasets become available.
  • Contribute to a future in which knowledge gained from studying Earth can help humanity prepare for exploration beyond our planet.

WHAT TOOLS DID WE USE TO CREATE OUR PROJECT?

UI/UX DESIGN:

HTML5 and CSS3, with a custom in-code design system featuring Inter and Playfair Display typography, glassmorphism components, responsive layouts, and interactive visual elements. Claude by Anthropic assisted with design iteration and refinement. Playwright was used for automated layout, accessibility, and responsive testing.

DEVELOPMENT:

Vanilla JavaScript (ES Modules), HTML5, CSS3, Python 3, and Node.js. Service Workers and IndexedDB support offline functionality, while Web Crypto provides SHA-256 data integrity verification. Git and GitHub were used for version control and collaboration, with GitHub Pages for deployment. Testing included pytest, Node.js test scripts, and Playwright. Claude Code served as the AI-assisted coding environment.

DATA PROCESSING AND ANALYSIS:

Python, NumPy, pandas, rasterio, netCDF4, Shapely, pyshp, Pillow, and Zarr. Data acquisition and processing involved NASA POWER API, NASA GIBS (WMS), NASA Earthdata CMR, and NASA Planetary Data System archives. ASTERRO's deterministic, versioned scoring engine (tai-sim-1.0.0) supports reproducible environmental comparisons, documented processing workflows, and SHA-256 provenance verification.

AI-ASSISTED DEVELOPMENT AND RESEARCH:

Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.2, and Claude Code by Anthropic; ChatGPT 6 Astra; ChatGPT 5.6 Sol, Luna, and Terra. These AI tools supported software development, technical problem-solving, research assistance, scientific explanations, analytical refinement, project documentation, and creative development. ASTERRO's Research Copilot also integrates the Anthropic API to assist users with planetary analogue research.

3D DESIGN AND VISUALISATION:

Custom WebGL-based 3D globe with shaders, alongside HTML Canvas 2D and SVG for interactive maps, radar fingerprints, charts, and environmental data layers. Visualisation textures include NASA Blue Marble, MGS MOLA, and LRO LOLA datasets.

VIDEO EDITING:

CapCut for video editing, sequencing, transitions, and final production. Higgsfield for AI-assisted visual and cinematic generation, Claude for scriptwriting and creative refinement, and ElevenLabs v2 for AI-generated voiceover. Playwright and Chromium were used for rendering project visuals, while FFmpeg supported video assembly and processing.

USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI)


AI tools were used throughout ASTERRO's research, development, design, visualization and communication workflows. Each tool supported specific stages of production, from technical problem-solving to cinematic presentation.

1. Claude Opus 5.5
Used as an advanced development and reasoning assistant for software architecture, implementation planning, complex technical problem-solving, code refinement and reviewing application logic. It also supported the development of research workflows and technical documentation. Its inputs included project requirements, application code, system architecture and relevant scientific documentation.

2. Claude Fable 5.2
Used for creative development, visual storytelling, narrative refinement, creative direction and production concepts. It helped shape presentation materials and communicate ASTERRO's scientific purpose. Its inputs included project descriptions, feature documentation, visual references and presentation requirements.

3. Higgsfield AI
Used for cinematic visual production, AI-assisted video generation, visual concepts, motion design and promotional storytelling. Its inputs included ASTERRO's project identity, creative prompts, planetary themes and visual references.

4. ElevenLabs v2
Used to generate AI-assisted voiceover narration for project presentation videos. The generated speech was based on our original written scripts and narration direction.

5. ChatGPT 6 Astra
Used for advanced reasoning, scientific and technical analysis, project strategy, system design discussions and complex problem-solving. Its inputs included project documentation, technical requirements, datasets and implementation details.

6. ChatGPT 5.6 Sol
Used for creative direction, storytelling, presentation development, visual concepts and refining communication materials. Its inputs included project descriptions, scripts and design references.

7. ChatGPT 5.6 Luna
Used for technical assistance, structured analysis, documentation, research organization and evaluating project features. Its inputs included application requirements, project information and relevant scientific materials.

8. ChatGPT 5.6 Terra
Used for additional reasoning, technical review, scientific communication, content refinement and exploring alternative approaches to project development. Its inputs included project documentation, environmental data descriptions and development requirements.

The AI tools assisted with development, reasoning, communication and media production; they were not treated as substitutes for scientific observations or authoritative datasets. ASTERRO's environmental analysis is based on documented NASA and partner data sources, including NASA POWER, MODIS, MOLA, MEDA, LOLA and Diviner, alongside USGS/NGA GMTED2010.

The platform's baseline analogue rankings are produced by its deterministic scoring engine using measurable environmental dimensions. AI-generated content was not presented as measured planetary observations or independently verified scientific evidence.

All AI-assisted outputs were subject to human direction, review and integration into the project.
